newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE - Want to hate someone in Venezuela? Hate a judge.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Want to hate someone in Venezuela? Hate a judge.

text.p: Judges are rarely thought of as the life and soul of a party, but in Venezuela they are actively shunned.
"Everyone just assumes they're corrupt," one U.S.-educated lawyer from a prestigious Caracas law firm said.
Venezuela's legal system has rarely looked sorrier. Grossly inefficient, heavily politicized and famously corrupt, even Justice Minister Henrique Meier admits it is "terrible ... Kafka-esque".

Undeterred, the World Bank has adopted Venezuela for its flagship judicial reform programme. In a country that adds new weight to the gypsy curse "may I see you among lawyers," no one doubts the Herculean scale of the task. "Here if you have a problem -- business or whatever -- you get your lawyer to get a judge to issue a writ, which solves the problem," a foreign businessman said.

In one celebrated case last year dubbed "the night it rained money," a female judge, ambushed by the police, allegedly hurled a cash bribe out of her 20th floor apartment. She later claimed she was only acting as a Robin Hood.
"I think she meant robbing hood," snorted a lawyer.

It was to help clean up this mess that the World Bank approved a $30 million loan in 1992. The project reflects a shift in the bank's focus from promoting sound economic policies that make up the free market to strengthening rules and institutions that safeguard them.
"The project is a bit like the forces of the Enlightenment slugging it out with the Spanish Inquisition," one experienced Venezuelan litigator said.

The apparent random vengefulness of Venezuelan justice stems from an agreement hammered out between the two main political parties in 1960 to divide up the country's main institutions, including judges and their favours. Badly paid judges deciding alone, without the countervailing force of juries, in Byzantine court rooms stacked with trial papers only add scope to the possibilities for corruption.

Inefficiency is such that an estimated one million cases are pending. Civil cases take an average 783 working days to process and penal cases almost twice as long. Three of every four of Venezuela's 24,000 prisoners are awaiting trial in jails infamous for terrible overcrowding and violence.

At least 25 inmates died in a fire this week that officials said was started by national guardsmen who lobbed incendiary devices and tear gas into an overcrowded cell at La Planta prison outside the capital.

While the innocent suffer in Venezuela, the guilty often walk free and frustration increasingly is leading Venezuelans to take justice into their own hands. "If justice doesn't act, we shall," reads a graffiti in one of Caracas's toughest neighbourhoods, Brisas de Propatria.

World Bank official Waleed Malik approaches the problem with an engineer's eye. He believes incremental change can finally produce big results. "Reform is not necessarily about changing laws but rather about making what there is work better," he told Reuters.
Whereas plaintiffs currently choose their own judges, a computerized system that randomly allocates cases has already shown positive early results, he said.
Model courts are to be set up early next year and their best practices disseminated in the country. Better training will be provided and the court bureaucracy reorganized.
Critics say a more drastic overhaul is needed. Some even suggest wholesale dismissals. But such fundamental change would require government action, which is improbable although not inconceivable.
Judicial reform holds centre stage in Venezuelan public debate, largely thanks to the bank's project. President Rafael Caldera has made the fight against corruption a personal goal.

But years of similar promises have left many Venezuelans sceptical of the will to change. "I wish them the best," said the litigator with a sigh. "However, I cannot but think it's an impossible dream."
